tagline: Follow an old Red River channel through farmland and Creole architecture.
intro: The Cane River National Heritage Trail Scenic Byway follows the water through farmland and small towns from Natchitoches to Cloutierville. Corn and soybean fields, sugar cane and pecan orchards border the old Red River channel. Louisiana’s byway program presents this 71-mile drive through its Creole architecture, plantation buildings and historic landmarks, allowing two days for a self-guided tour.

Natchitoches was a French trading outpost, and cotton from east Texas later moved here from land transport to boats bound for New Orleans. When the Red River changed course, it bypassed the town and severed its connection to the Mississippi. In the 1970s, Mayor Bobby DeBlieux promoted historic preservation as a way to revive the town, supporting both a historic district and a national park at Oakland and Magnolia plantations.

Begin in Natchitoches, then head south to Natchez and Oakland Plantation, where the national park interprets the lives of planters and enslaved workers. The national park’s exhibits include slave cabins and corn cribs as well as plantation houses. Melrose follows, with the plantation where Clementine Hunter worked and painted rural Louisiana life. Finish at Cloutierville, whose main street includes St. John’s Catholic Church and tenant houses from 1880 to 1930.

moments.title: Natchitoches
moments.text: Front Street’s bricks were lifted one at a time during restoration, numbered and cleaned before workers put them back after repairing the utilities, drainage and foundation beneath. The street overlooks the river walk in the historic district. Natchitoches began in 1714 as a French outpost for trade with Spanish-controlled Mexico, near a village of Natchitoches Indians whose name the city took. The change in the Red River’s course left Cane River Lake where the shipping channel had been. Its preserved architecture includes wrought iron, stucco and red brick, with Front Street itself retaining its brick paving.
moments.notice: Front Street retains brick paving; wrought iron, stucco and red brick also appear in the city’s architecture.

moments.title: Oakland Plantation
moments.text: Oakland occupies a bend of Cane River Lake, with a mule barn, turkey shed and two pigeon houses among its surviving farm buildings. By 1860, the Prud’homme plantation held 160 enslaved African Americans who harvested cotton, worked in the house and made tools and furniture. After the Civil War, sharecroppers, primarily descendants of those enslaved here, farmed small plots and lived in the cabins. Mechanization in the 1960s ended that system; tenants were asked to leave. The National Park Service acquired the main buildings and surrounding land in 1997. The park interprets emancipation and the lives of freedmen, Creoles of color and their descendants who continued working here after the Civil War.

moments.title: Melrose Plantation
moments.text: Louis Metoyer’s son completed Melrose’s Big House in 1833, after his father’s death. The Metoyers were free people of color who also enslaved others. Clementine Hunter later lived and worked at Melrose, becoming a self-taught artist whose paintings recorded Black Southern life. Her subjects included plantation work, domestic chores, funerals, baptisms and weddings. Hunter also made quilts and other textiles; many quilts depicted buildings on the Melrose grounds. In 1955, she and François Mignon collaborated on nine mural panels depicting Cane River Valley history and her own life. Each panel was painted in her home studio.
